warmup.q: A service on virtual threads handles each incoming payment in its own virtual thread and calls a card issuer that allows 50 concurrent requests. A traffic spike brings 5,000 payments at once. What protects the issuer?
options: Nothing is needed: virtual threads are cheap, so 5,000 calls are fine
The JVM limits virtual threads to the number of CPU cores
A semaphore bulkhead of 50 around the issuer call
warmup.why: Virtual threads remove the cost of threads, not the limits of what they call. Thousands of them will happily send thousands of concurrent requests. The JVM runs them on a few carrier threads, but a blocked virtual thread unmounts, so all 5,000 can be waiting on the issuer at once. A bulkhead (a semaphore with tryAcquire) caps the in-flight calls at what the issuer allows.

sections.html:
The safest way to share work between threads is to share a queue and nothing else. In producer-consumer, producers put work into a BlockingQueue, consumers take it out, and the queue does all the locking and waiting:

Java
BlockingQueue<Msg> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16);           // bounded: a full queue makes the producer wait
for (int c = 0; c < 4; c++) {
    pool.submit(() -> {
        while (true) {
            if (queue.take() instanceof Stop) return null;          // poison pill: this consumer is done
            processed.incrementAndGet();
        }
    });
}
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) queue.put(new Job(i));
for (int c = 0; c < 4; c++) queue.put(new Stop());                  // one pill PER consumer
Kotlin
val channel = Channel<Int>(capacity = 16)                          // bounded: send suspends when full
val workers = List(4) {
    launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
        for (job in channel) processed.incrementAndGet()            // ends when the channel is closed and drained
    }
}
repeat(1_000) { channel.send(it) }
channel.close()                                                     // one call stops every worker

Three rules from Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers still hold. Bound the queue: a full ArrayBlockingQueue(16) makes a fast producer wait, which is backpressure, while an unbounded queue hides overload until the heap runs out. Send one poison pill per consumer, because each pill stops exactly one. And don't swallow InterruptedException: it is how a pool tells its workers to stop. Kotlin's channel removes the pill: close() ends every for (job in channel) loop once the buffer is empty. Use a for loop in each worker, not consumeEach, which cancels the channel when its own loop ends.

A worker pool is the same picture with the queue inside an ExecutorService. A fixed pool of platform threads still suits CPU-bound work. For blocking I/O, Java 21 brought back thread-per-message: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a virtual thread for every task, and Kotlin launches a coroutine per message. Both make it trivial to send ten thousand concurrent requests to a PSP that accepts fifty, so thread-per-message always comes with a limit. That limit is the bulkhead, two sections down.

try.title: Forget a poison pill
steps: Run ProducerConsumerDemo (Java or Kotlin) with the command below.
Java: replace the pill loop with a single queue.put(new Stop());. Kotlin: delete channel.close(). Predict both numbers in the output line, then run.

code.title: ProducerConsumerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** One producer, four consumers, a bounded queue, and one poison pill per consumer. */ public class ProducerConsumerDemo { sealed interface Msg permits Job, Stop {} record Job(int id) implements Msg {} record Stop() implements Msg {} public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int consumers = 4, jobs = 1_000; BlockingQueue<Msg> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16); // bounded: a full queue makes the producer wait AtomicInteger processed = new AtomicInteger(); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) { pool.submit(() -> { while (true) { Msg m = queue.take(); if (m instanceof Stop) return null; // this consumer is done processed.incrementAndGet(); } }); } for (int i = 0; i < jobs; i++) queue.put(new Job(i)); for (int c = 0; c < consumers; c++) queue.put(new Stop()); // one pill PER consumer pool.shutdown(); boolean finished = pool.awaitTermination(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println("processed " + processed + " of " + jobs + ", all consumers finished: " + finished); if (!finished) { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupt the ones still blocked in take() System.out.println("some consumers never got a pill and were still waiting in take()"); } } }

alt.title: ProducerConsumerDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds // One producer, four consumers, a bounded channel, and close() as the poison pill for all of them. fun main() = runBlocking { val jobs = 1_000 val channel = Channel<Int>(capacity = 16) // bounded: send suspends when full val processed = AtomicInteger() val workers = List(4) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { for (job in channel) processed.incrementAndGet() // ends when the channel is closed and drained } } repeat(jobs) { channel.send(it) } channel.close() // one call stops every worker val finished = withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { workers.joinAll() } != null println("processed $processed of $jobs, all workers finished: $finished") if (!finished) { workers.forEach { it.cancel() } println("the workers were still waiting to receive: nobody closed the channel") } }

try.expect: processed 1000 of 1000, all consumers finished: true. With one pill, all 1,000 jobs are still processed, but after the two-second wait the line reads all consumers finished: false, and the demo reports that consumers were still waiting in take(). Three of the four never got a pill. In Kotlin without close(), the workers wait forever for the next element: all workers finished: false. In a service, that is a shutdown that hangs.

sections.h: Who owns the state: the patterns you already know
sections.html:
Most of the remaining concurrency patterns answer one question: who owns this state, and what happens to callers who arrive at the wrong moment? You've met them all in earlier tracks:

Pattern Problem Java 21+ Kotlin Taught in
Immutable object share state with no locks records with List.copyOf data class with vals and copied lists Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal
Active object one owner for mutable state a single-thread executor as a mailbox; methods return CompletableFuture a coroutine that owns the state and reads commands from a Channel Observer and Command (the command worker)
Guarded suspension wait until a condition holds wait() in a while loop, or better CompletableFuture, CountDownLatch, Condition CompletableDeferred.await(), which suspends wait, notify and guarded blocks
Balking don't start if it's already running AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) the same, or Mutex.tryLock() Atomics and compare-and-set
Read-write lock many readers, rare writers ReentrantReadWriteLock (no read-to-write upgrade), or an AtomicReference to an immutable snapshot the same Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock
Future / promise a result that arrives later CompletableFuture with your own executor async and await inside coroutineScope CompletableFuture: composing async steps

Balking is the one people get wrong most often. A settlement job that runs on a schedule, on retries and from an operator's button must never run twice at once. If it is already running, the right answer is to return at once, not to wait:

Java
final class SettlementJob {
    private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean();

    boolean runIfIdle(Runnable settle) {
        if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false;      // balk: a run is in progress
        try {
            settle.run();
            return true;
        } finally {
            running.set(false);
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class SettlementJob {
    private val mutex = Mutex()

    suspend fun runIfIdle(settle: suspend () -> Unit): Boolean {
        if (!mutex.tryLock()) return false                          // balk: a run is in progress
        try {
            settle()
            return true
        } finally {
            mutex.unlock()
        }
    }
}

The plain-boolean version, if (running) return; running = true;, is check-then-act and lets two runs overlap. And an AtomicBoolean protects one JVM only. With three pods, each pod has its own flag, so a run that must be unique across the fleet needs a database lock or a lease.

try.title: Turn the balk into check-then-act
steps: Run SettlementJobDemo in either language: eight triggers fire at the same moment. Read the line.

Replace the compareAndSet line with three lines: if (running.get()) return false;, then for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); (Kotlin: repeat(1_000) { Thread.onSpinWait() }), then running.set(true);.
Run it four or five times and watch most runs at once. Then restore the compareAndSet.

code.title: SettlementJobDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Balking: eight triggers fire at once, and the settlement run refuses to start while one is in progress. */ public class SettlementJobDemo { static final class SettlementJob { private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(); boolean runIfIdle(Runnable settle) { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false; // balk: a run is already in progress try { settle.run(); return true; } finally { running.set(false); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { SettlementJob job = new SettlementJob(); AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger(), mostAtOnce = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger ran = new AtomicInteger(), balked = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable settle = () -> { mostAtOnce.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // settling takes a moment inside.decrementAndGet(); }; CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] triggers = new Thread[8]; // the scheduler, a retry, an operator's button... for (int t = 0; t < triggers.length; t++) { triggers[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } if (job.runIfIdle(settle)) ran.incrementAndGet(); else balked.incrementAndGet(); }); triggers[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : triggers) t.join(); System.out.println("ran " + ran + ", balked " + balked + ", most runs at once: " + mostAtOnce); } }

alt.title: SettlementJobDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l11 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Balking: eight triggers fire at once, and the settlement run refuses to start while one is in progress. class SettlementJob { private val running = AtomicBoolean() fun runIfIdle(settle: () -> Unit): Boolean { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false // balk: a run is already in progress try { settle() return true } finally { running.set(false) } } } fun main() { val job = SettlementJob() val inside = AtomicInteger() val mostAtOnce = AtomicInteger() val ran = AtomicInteger() val balked = AtomicInteger() val settle = { mostAtOnce.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) repeat(2_000_000) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // settling takes a moment inside.decrementAndGet() Unit } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val triggers = List(8) { // the scheduler, a retry, an operator's button... thread { go.await() if (job.runIfIdle(settle)) ran.incrementAndGet() else balked.incrementAndGet() } } go.countDown() triggers.forEach { it.join() } println("ran $ran, balked $balked, most runs at once: $mostAtOnce") }

try.expect: With compareAndSet, most runs at once is always 1, and usually ran 1, balked 7. With check-then-act, several triggers pass the check before any of them sets the flag, so most runs print 2 or 3 for most runs at once: two settlement runs over the same batch at the same time. It is the race from the concurrency track, inside a pattern.

sections.h: Bulkhead: cap the calls to each dependency
sections.html:
Virtual threads make threads cheap. They don't make your dependencies cheap. The card issuer accepts 50 concurrent requests, the Oracle pool has 20 connections, and the fraud service slows to a crawl above 100. A bulkhead caps how many calls run against one dependency at once, so a slow dependency can use up its own share and nothing else. The name comes from ships: watertight walls keep one leak from flooding the hull.

Java
final class Bulkhead {
    private final Semaphore permits;
    Bulkhead(int maxConcurrent) { permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); }

    <T> T call(Supplier<T> op) {
        if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw new BulkheadFull();     // fail fast: don't queue behind slow calls
        try {
            return op.get();
        } finally {
            permits.release();                                    // always, or the limit shrinks for good
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class Bulkhead(maxConcurrent: Int) {
    private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent)                // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore

    suspend fun <T> call(op: suspend () -> T): T {
        if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFull()           // fail fast: don't queue behind slow calls
        try {
            return op()
        } finally {
            permits.release()                                     // always, or the limit shrinks for good
        }
    }
}

tryAcquire() makes the bulkhead fail fast: a call over the limit gets an error at once instead of waiting behind the slow ones. Resilience4j's semaphore bulkhead does the same by default (maxConcurrentCalls = 25, maxWaitDuration = 0). acquire() would wait, which turns the bulkhead into a limiter. That's fine for a batch job, and risky on a request path, where waiting requests pile up until the caller times out.

Size each bulkhead to its dependency, not to your threads. A bulkhead of 30 in front of a 20-connection pool still queues ten callers inside the pool. With virtual threads, a semaphore is the natural limiter (Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores); a separate thread pool per dependency brings back the pools that virtual threads let you drop. Spring Framework 7 ships the same idea as @ConcurrencyLimit, applied through a proxy, so the self-invocation rule from Decorator and Proxy applies to it.

try.title: Wait for a permit, or fail fast
steps: Run BulkheadDemo (Java or Kotlin). It sends 200 calls that each take 20 ms through a 20-permit semaphore, first with acquire() (wait), then with tryAcquire() (fail fast). Predict both lines first.
Change the semaphore from 20 permits to 200 and run again. Predict most in flight before you look.

code.title: BulkheadDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 200 virtual threads call a PSP that should see at most 20 at once: wait for a permit, or fail fast. */ public class BulkheadDemo { static void run(String mode, boolean failFast) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(20); AtomicInteger inFlight = new AtomicInteger(), mostInFlight = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger done = new AtomicInteger(), rejected = new AtomicInteger(); long start = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { ex.submit(() -> { if (failFast) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); return null; } // bulkhead: reject now } else { permits.acquire(); // limiter: wait in line } try { mostInFlight.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); Thread.sleep(20); // the PSP takes 20 ms inFlight.decrementAndGet(); done.incrementAndGet(); } finally { permits.release(); } return null; }); } } // close() waits for all tasks long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-10s done %3d, rejected %3d, most in flight %2d, about %d ms%n", mode, done.get(), rejected.get(), mostInFlight.get(), ms); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("wait", false); run("fail fast", true); } }

alt.title: BulkheadDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger // 200 coroutines call a PSP that should see at most 20 at once: wait for a permit, or fail fast. suspend fun runBulkhead(mode: String, failFast: Boolean) { val permits = Semaphore(20) val inFlight = AtomicInteger() val mostInFlight = AtomicInteger() val done = AtomicInteger() val rejected = AtomicInteger() val start = System.nanoTime() coroutineScope { // waits for all 200 children repeat(200) { launch { if (failFast) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); return@launch } // bulkhead: reject now } else { permits.acquire() // limiter: wait in line } try { mostInFlight.accumulateAndGet(inFlight.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) delay(20) // the PSP takes 20 ms inFlight.decrementAndGet() done.incrementAndGet() } finally { permits.release() } } } } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 println("%-10s done %3d, rejected %3d, most in flight %2d, about %d ms".format(mode, done.get(), rejected.get(), mostInFlight.get(), ms)) } fun main() = runBlocking { runBulkhead("wait", failFast = false) runBulkhead("fail fast", failFast = true) }

try.expect: Waiting: done 200, rejected 0, most in flight 20, in a bit over 200 ms (ten waves of 20). Fail fast: about done 20, rejected 180, in about 20 ms. The exact split can vary slightly between runs. With 200 permits, most in flight jumps to 200 in both modes: nothing protects the PSP. Your times will differ a little from these.

sections.h: Circuit breaker: State, Decorator and compare-and-set in one class
sections.html:
A bulkhead limits how much a failing dependency can hurt you. A circuit breaker stops calling it for a while. After a run of failures the breaker opens, and calls fail at once without a network trip. That gives the issuer room to recover and gives your callers a quick answer instead of a two-second timeout. After a cool-down the breaker goes half-open and lets one probe through: success closes it, failure opens it again.

The breaker is this track's capstone, because it is three earlier patterns in one class. Its states are sealed records with a transition, as in State and Chain of Responsibility. Its call(op) wraps any operation behind the same shape, as a decorator does. And its state lives in an AtomicReference that changes by compare-and-set, so a thousand request threads can share it without a lock:

Java
sealed interface State permits Closed, Open, HalfOpen {}
record Closed(int consecutiveFailures) implements State {}
record Open(Instant until) implements State {}
record HalfOpen() implements State {}

private final AtomicReference<State> state = new AtomicReference<>(new Closed(0));

// after a failed call: one pure transition, applied atomically
state.updateAndGet(cur -> switch (cur) {
    case HalfOpen h -> new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor));                            // the probe failed
    case Closed(var n) when n + 1 >= threshold -> new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor)); // trip
    case Closed(var n) -> new Closed(n + 1);
    case Open o -> o;                                                                      // already open
});
Kotlin
sealed interface State {
    data class Closed(val consecutiveFailures: Int) : State
    data class Open(val until: Instant) : State
    data object HalfOpen : State
}

private val state = AtomicReference<State>(State.Closed(0))

// after a failed call: one pure transition, applied atomically
state.updateAndGet { cur ->
    when (cur) {
        State.HalfOpen -> State.Open(clock.instant() + openFor)                                     // the probe failed
        is State.Closed if cur.consecutiveFailures + 1 >= threshold -> State.Open(clock.instant() + openFor)   // trip
        is State.Closed -> State.Closed(cur.consecutiveFailures + 1)
        is State.Open -> cur                                                                        // already open
    }
}

Two choices make it testable and correct. Time comes from an injected Clock, so a test moves time forward 31 seconds at once instead of sleeping. And the move from open to half-open is a compareAndSet: when the cool-down ends and many threads arrive together, exactly one wins the right to probe, and the rest are still rejected.

In production, use a library. Resilience4j 2.4.0 adds sliding windows, failure-rate and slow-call thresholds, metrics and events. Learn its defaults before you trust a test: minimumNumberOfCalls is 100, so a breaker that fails five calls in a unit test never opens, and waitDurationInOpenState is 60 seconds. And decide what counts as a failure. A declined card means the issuer is working fine, so it must not trip the breaker.

figure.caption: The breaker's three states. Only one probe runs in half-open; its result decides whether the breaker closes or opens again.

analogy: Picture a restaurant kitchen. The order rail is producer-consumer: waiters clip tickets on, cooks take them off, and a full rail tells the waiters to slow down. Each station has four burners, so a run on soup can't take the grill's burners: a bulkhead. When the fryer catches fire, someone hangs a sign saying "no fried food for ten minutes", and orders that need it are refused at the door instead of waiting forever: the breaker opening. When the dishwasher is already running, nobody starts a second one: balking. The analogy breaks on knowing why. A kitchen can see the fire. A breaker only counts failures, so you must tell it which errors mean "the dependency is sick" and which, like a declined card, mean the dependency is working perfectly.
world: Your Kafka consumers are producer-consumer at the scale of a cluster: partitions are the queues, and a consumer per partition is the confinement that keeps per-account ordering safe. Your Quarkus services already speak these patterns through SmallRye Fault Tolerance's @CircuitBreaker, @Bulkhead, @Retry and @Timeout, which are interceptor-based, so they need calls that go through the proxy. Temporal brings its own retry policy for activities: don't add a second retry around the PSP call inside the activity, or one failure becomes nine calls. And breakers are per instance: with six pods, each pod has its own breaker and its own view of the issuer, so the fleet keeps probing a dead issuer six times as often as one pod would.
mistake: The most common mistake is retrying at every layer. The mobile app retries three times, the API gateway retries three times, the payment service's client retries three times, and Temporal retries the activity. One user tap becomes dozens of calls to an issuer that is already struggling, and the retries keep it down. It happens because each team adds a retry to make their own layer reliable, and nobody sees the product. Retry in one place, close to the call, only for idempotent operations or with an idempotency key, with backoff and jitter. Never retry a CallNotPermitted or a full bulkhead: those mean "stop", not "try again".

compare.title: Guarded suspension: waiting for a 3-D Secure callback

java.title: ChallengeResults.java
java.html: // the request thread waits until the issuer's webhook arrives, or gives up after a timeout final class ChallengeResults { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> pending = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String awaitResult(String paymentId, Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException, TimeoutException { CompletableFuture<String> slot = pending.computeIfAbsent(paymentId, id -> new CompletableFuture<>()); try { return slot.get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // blocks this thread until completed } finally { pending.remove(paymentId); } } // the webhook thread completes the guard; a callback that comes first is kept for the waiter void onCallback(String paymentId, String result) { pending.computeIfAbsent(paymentId, id -> new CompletableFuture<>()).complete(result); } }

kotlin.title: ChallengeResults.kt
kotlin.html: // the request coroutine waits until the issuer's webhook arrives, or gives up after a timeout class ChallengeResults { private val pending = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableDeferred<String>>() suspend fun awaitResult(paymentId: String, timeout: Duration): String { val slot = pending.computeIfAbsent(paymentId) { CompletableDeferred() } try { return withTimeout(timeout) { slot.await() } // suspends: no thread is held while waiting } finally { pending.remove(paymentId) } } // the webhook handler completes the guard; a callback that comes first is kept for the waiter fun onCallback(paymentId: String, result: String) { pending.computeIfAbsent(paymentId) { CompletableDeferred() }.complete(result) } }

compare.note: Both replace the hand-written wait() in a while loop with a one-shot promise, which can't miss a signal or wake up spuriously: complete happens once, and get or await returns as soon as it has. The difference is what waiting costs. CompletableFuture.get blocks a thread; on a virtual thread that is cheap, but it is still a thread per waiting payment. CompletableDeferred.await suspends the coroutine and holds no thread at all, and withTimeout cancels the wait cleanly. Java needs three checked exceptions in the signature; Kotlin needs none, and the timeout arrives as a TimeoutCancellationException. One gap is shared: a callback that arrives after the waiter gave up leaves an entry in the map, so a real version also expires old entries.

worked.title: Put retry, breaker and bulkhead in the right order

steps.say: Three pieces from this lesson wrap one PSP charge. The order of the wrappers decides what happens on a bad day. Before reading on: with retry outermost, what does each retry attempt do while the breaker is open?
steps.code: Supplier<String> charge = () -> psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250); // idempotency key Supplier<String> limited = () -> bulkhead.call(charge); // innermost: caps the calls in flight to the PSP Supplier<String> guarded = () -> breaker.call(limited); // then: stop calling a PSP that keeps failing String ref = retrying(3, guarded); // outermost: try again on transient failures

alt.html: val charge = Supplier { psp.charge("order-7781:charge", "tok_42", 1_250) } // idempotency key val limited = Supplier { bulkhead.call(charge) } // innermost: caps the calls in flight to the PSP val guarded = Supplier { breaker.call(limited) } // then: stop calling a PSP that keeps failing val ref = retrying(3) { guarded.get() } // outermost: try again on transient failures

steps.say: Each attempt hits the open breaker and gets CallNotPermitted in microseconds, which costs the PSP nothing. But a rejection isn't a transient failure, and retrying it is noise. Teach the retry to let fail-fast signals through untouched.
steps.code: static <T> T retrying(int attempts, Supplier<T> body) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return body.get(); } catch (CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted | Bulkhead.BulkheadFull e) { throw e; // 1. fail-fast signals: never retry them } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; // 2. a timeout or a 503: worth another attempt } } throw last; }

alt.html: inline fun <T> retrying(attempts: Int, body: () -> T): T { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return body() } catch (e: CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted) { throw e // 1. fail-fast signals: never retry them } catch (e: Bulkhead.BulkheadFull) { throw e } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e // 2. a timeout or a 503: worth another attempt } } throw last!! }

steps.say: Why is the bulkhead inside the breaker? An open breaker rejects before the bulkhead is reached, so a dead PSP never holds permits. Why is the retry outside? Each attempt is a separate breaker call, so three failed attempts count as three failures, and a PSP that is really down trips the breaker within one or two payments. Retrying inside the breaker would hide those failures from it.
steps.code:
what each layer sees for one payment while the PSP returns 503:

retry      attempt 1          attempt 2          attempt 3
breaker    Closed(0) -> (1)   Closed(1) -> (2)   Closed(2) -> Open    (three failures trip it)
bulkhead   permit, released   permit, released   permit, released

next payment: retry -> breaker rejects at once (CallNotPermitted) -> no PSP call, no permit

steps.say: Pin it in a test with a fake PSP that always fails and the lab's classes. The second payment must never reach the PSP.
steps.code: AtomicInteger pspCalls = new AtomicInteger(); Supplier<String> failing = () -> { pspCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw new IllegalStateException("PSP 503"); }; CircuitBreaker breaker = new CircuitBreaker(3, Duration.ofSeconds(30), clock); Bulkhead bulkhead = new Bulkhead(20); Supplier<String> pipeline = () -> breaker.call(() -> bulkhead.call(failing)); assertThatThrownBy(() -> retrying(3, pipeline)).hasMessage("PSP 503"); // 4. first payment: 3 attempts assertThat(breaker.state()).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.Open.class); assertThatThrownBy(() -> retrying(3, pipeline)).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted.class); assertThat(pspCalls.get()).isEqualTo(3); // 5. the second never left

lab.title: A circuit breaker with a fake clock, and a semaphore bulkhead
steps: Read the state table in the Javadoc of CircuitBreaker; the states, the constructor and state() are given. Run the tests: all ten fail.

Write the first half of call: read the state. If it is Open and the clock is still before until, throw CallNotPermitted. If the cool-down is over, compareAndSet it to HalfOpen, and throw if you lose. If it is already HalfOpen, throw.

Write the second half: run op. On success, move to Closed(0) unless another thread has opened the breaker meanwhile. On a RuntimeException, apply the failure transition with updateAndGet and rethrow the same exception.
Run the tests until all ten pass, then run them twice more. Concurrency code has to pass every time.
hints: if (s instanceof Open(var until)) gives you until in one step. state.compareAndSet(s, new HalfOpen()) succeeds only if nobody changed the state since you read s, so exactly one thread becomes the probe.
On success, state.updateAndGet(cur -> cur instanceof Open ? cur : new Closed(0)) closes both a half-open breaker and a closed one with failures, without undoing an open set by another thread.
The failure transition is the four-case switch from the lesson: HalfOpen and the tripping Closed both become new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor)).
lab.done: All ten tests in ResilienceTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A fail-fast bulkhead from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a Bulkhead that lets at most n calls run at once and rejects the rest immediately with an exception. Then answer two questions: what goes wrong if you release() outside a finally, and what changes if you use acquire() instead of tryAcquire()?

answer.html: final class Bulkhead { static final class BulkheadFull extends RuntimeException {} private final Semaphore permits; Bulkhead(int n) { permits = new Semaphore(n); } <T> T call(Supplier<T> op) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw new BulkheadFull(); // fail fast; acquire() would wait in line try { return op.get(); } finally { permits.release(); // outside finally, every exception leaks a permit until none are left } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class Bulkhead(n: Int) { class BulkheadFull : RuntimeException() private val permits = Semaphore(n) // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore suspend fun <T> call(op: suspend () -> T): T { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFull() // fail fast; acquire() would suspend in line try { return op() } finally { permits.release() // outside finally, every exception leaks a permit until none are left } } }

recap: Producer-consumer: share a bounded queue and nothing else. One poison pill per consumer in Java; close() the channel in Kotlin, and use for, not consumeEach, in each worker.
Thread-per-message is back with virtual threads and coroutines, but cheap threads make it easy to flood a dependency, so it always comes with a limit.
Balking returns at once when the object is busy. Use compareAndSet (or Mutex.tryLock), never a check-then-act on a plain boolean, and remember it only covers one JVM.
A bulkhead is a semaphore per dependency with tryAcquire: it fails fast, releases in finally, and is sized to the dependency, not to your threads.
A circuit breaker is State plus Decorator plus compare-and-set: sealed states in an AtomicReference, a call(op) wrapper, an injected Clock, and one half-open probe chosen by compareAndSet.
Retry in one layer only, around idempotent calls, outside the breaker, and never on CallNotPermitted or a full bulkhead.

explain.prompt: Explain how the lab's circuit breaker combines State, Decorator and compare-and-set, and why the move from open to half-open has to be a compareAndSet.
explain.answer: The breaker's state is a small sealed type, Closed(failures), Open(until) and HalfOpen, and each outcome moves it with a pure transition, like the payment state machine. That's State. Its call(op) takes any operation and returns that operation's result through the same shape, adding behavior around it, which is what a decorator does. The current state lives in an AtomicReference so that hundreds of request threads can share one breaker without a lock, and every change is a compare-and-set or updateAndGet. The open-to-half-open move matters most. When the cool-down ends, many threads may read the same expired Open state at once. compareAndSet(thatOpen, new HalfOpen()) succeeds for exactly one of them, which becomes the probe; the others see their CAS fail and are rejected. With a plain set, every one of them would probe a PSP that may still be down. The injected Clock is what lets the tests check all this without sleeping.

deeper.html:
Resilience4j's breaker defaults, read from its source and printed by version 2.4.0: failureRateThreshold 50%, slowCallRateThreshold 100%, slowCallDurationThreshold 60 s, waitDurationInOpenState 60 s, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState 10, minimumNumberOfCalls 100, and a count-based sliding window of 100 calls. Every exception counts as a failure unless you configure recordExceptions or ignoreExceptions. The project's README says Resilience4j 3 will require Java 21 and adds virtual-thread schedulers; it wasn't on Maven Central when this course was written, so the labs build the breaker by hand.

Spring Framework 7 added @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit to the core framework, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods. @Retryable defaults to maxRetries = 3 after the first failure, so four attempts in total, with a one-second delay. Both work through proxies, so the self-invocation rule applies.

Structured concurrency is the future-and-promise pattern with a lifetime. StructuredTaskScope forks subtasks, joins them, and cancels the rest when one fails, so no subtask outlives the method that started it. It is still a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27 (run with --enable-preview), which is why it stays out of the labs. Kotlin's coroutineScope has worked this way since the start: an async that fails cancels its siblings, and the scope waits for every child.

The patterns in this lesson have distributed cousins. A database row lock or a lease is balking across pods. Kafka partitions are producer-consumer with ordering per key. A Temporal workflow is an active object with durable state: one logical thread per workflow, commands in, results out. The questions you ask stay the same: who owns the state, what waits, and what fails fast.
